list.listitem: Glomerulonephritis (GN) is a group of uncommon and disparate diseases, usually immunologically mediated, with some common pathophysiologic and clinical features. C
Suspect GN with new-onset secondary hypertension, azotemia, hematuria with red blood cell (RBC) casts, or edema and proteinuria. C
GN may present as acute nephritic syndrome, as nephrotic syndrome, or as non-nephrotic proteinuria with/without hematuria. C
Diagnosis requires serologic testing and renal biopsy. C
Treatment depends on diagnosis but typically involves high-dose steroids and immunosuppressives, specific to the diagnosis; response is highly variable. B
Chronic and end-stage renal disease (ESRD) are common outcomes, but prognosis varies widely depending on the syndrome (). B

background.definition: Glomerulonephritis (GN) is a group of syndromes of acute renal dysfunction characterized by azotemia, hypertension, hematuria, RBC casts in the urine, and edema. Presentations include nephrotic syndrome (NS), acute nephritic syndrome, and asymptomatic hematuria of glomerular origin with or without proteinuria.

list.listitem: See .

Glomerulonephritis (GN) is classified in several ways: (1) focal nephritic versus diffuse nephritic versus nephrotic; (2) primary versus secondary; and (3) especially for primary, by pathologic description. Incidence varies somewhat by age.
For primary pathologies, many etiologies have been described, but most cases are idiopathic.
For postinfectious GN, many infections have been cited, but streptococcal infection is the classic.

Risk factors for most primary GN are unclear, although many patients have a viral syndrome in the preceding weeks. For secondary GN, several pathologic types are often described. The major risk factor for IgA nephropathy (most common GN in world) is viral hepatitis, but in the United States most cases are idiopathic. In SLE, about half of the patients have some renal involvement.
In light of newer molecular and genomic insights, reclassification in the near future is possible.
Glomerulonephritis results from immune mechanisms. Inciting factors are often not known, except in postinfectious disease or with certain toxins.

Complement activation and immunoglobulin deposition occur in an immune response with both humoral and cellular components. Target antigen may be localized in the glomerulus. Antibodies that induce immune deposits may be directed against normal constituents of the glomerulus, self-antigens of nonrenal origin, or exogenous antigens or immune complexes that localize in glomerular capillaries.

Deposits may form in the mesangium, or the inner capillary surface (subendothelial) or outer capillary surface (subepithelial). When the inflammatory response is excessively fierce or rapid, capillary wall destruction may occur with formation of crescents in Bowman's space.
Rate and degree of crescent formation are important determinants of prognosis.
There is no effective screening for primary glomerular disease. Routine urinalysis is not cost-effective. C
For secondary glomerulonephritis, employ the usual monitoring of the underlying primary disease process. C
Assess renal function, quantify proteinuria, and perform UA for RBCs and RBC casts. C

Serologies: C3, antinuclear antibodies (ANA), antineutrophilic cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA), hepatitis profile, anti-streptolysin O (ASO), anti-glomerular basement membrane (GBM) antibody, cryoglobulin, serum, and urine protein electrophoresis or immunofixation. C
All serologies may be negative. C
Renal biopsy is usually necessary for adults. C

Glomerulonephritis (GN): patients typically present with a change in character of urine and possibly with reduced output. They may have constitutional symptoms of fatigue or shortness of breath or be found to have hypertension, azotemia, and hematuria. Other findings on physical examination might suggest a secondary form of GN. Often there is a prodrome of a viral-like illness 3 to 6 weeks earlier, but this is a nonspecific and inconstant finding.

Nephrotic syndrome (NS): patients typically present with edema and foamy urine and may have hypertension and/or azotemia. Patients typically have hypoalbuminemia, dyslipidemia (elevated triglycerides and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol) and may have muscle wasting if proteinuria is of a significant degree or duration.
Onset is often insidious.
Diagnosis is often suspected because of abnormal BUN and creatinine in patients with nonspecific constitutional symptoms.
UA in GN: hematuria, low to moderate (trace to +++) proteinuria. RBC casts are virtually pathognomonic.
UA in nephrotic syndrome (NS): heavy proteinuria; sediment may be bland, may have Maltese crosses.
Level of suspicion directs the serologic work-up.

Serologies may include: C3 complement, ANA, ANCA (p- and c-), ASO (or equivalent); anti-GBM antibody, cryoglobulin, hepatitis profile, serum, and urine electrophoresis or immunofixation. All serologies might be negative.
Renal biopsy, the gold standard, must still be interpreted in light of serologies.
See .

Suspect glomerulonephritis (GN) in patients with new onset hypertension and tea- or cola-colored urine (possibly with decreased urine output); foamy urine may be seen in NS. Edema is minimal to moderate edema in GN and greater in NS.
Findings of primary disease (eg, rash or arthritis in SLE) suggests secondary GN.
Typical for acute nephritic syndrome: azotemia, hematuria, hypertension, RBC casts.
Typical for nephrotic syndrome: edema, proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, hyperlipidemia.
Treatment depends on pathologic diagnosis or primary and underlying disorder if secondary (see ); it often involves high-dose oral corticosteroids and immunosuppressives. B
Blood pressure (BP) control with an angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) or angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) is important. B
Novel treatments include apheresis and monoclonal antibodies. C
Specific therapy depends on the specific glomerular pathology (see ).
BP control is important in patients with chronic glomerulonephritis, with ACE or ARB as the preferred first-line antihypertensives. Either agent slows progression of renal dysfunction.
One RCT showed that the combination of an ACE and an ARB was more effective than an ARB alone to reduce proteinuria, but evidence regarding survival and ESRD is lacking.

Edema may cause symptomatic ascites, pleural effusions, or pulmonary edema, which must be treated appropriately with diuretics. Loop diuretics are recommended for BP, oliguria, and edema management. Avoid thiazide diuretics as first line (unless in combination with loop blockers for severe edema/oliguria).
Antiviral therapy for chronic hepatitis B and C associated glomerulonephritis may improve some renal outcomes, but is insufficient to use alone.
Use statins for dyslipidemia.
A low-sodium diet is recommended.
Low-protein diets have been used to retard progression of renal insufficiency and to reduce proteinuria; efficacy has not been clearly demonstrated.

Consider hospitalization for patients with malignant hypertension, acute kidney injury with oliguria/anuria, and complications of pulmonary edema (or in the case of secondary glomerulonephritis or primary pulmonary injury).

Also consider hospitalization for uremic complications (eg, pericarditis, intractable hyperkalemia), initiation of dialysis, or acute flair of primary disease (eg, lupus), and if IV methylprednisolone or immunosuppressives are needed.

If chronic kidney disease supervenes, the usual management considerations must be added to the patient's care, including BP control, lipid management, and treatment for anemia with iron and erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, and management of secondary hyperparathyroidism.
Each condition carries its own range of prognoses, with variability within each category (see ). B
Other variables may include age, gender, smoking, and family history for some diagnoses. C
Chronic and end-stage renal disease are common outcomes. B
Monitor BUN, creatinine, electrolytes, microscopic UA, and proteinuria (24-hour urine collection or spot urine protein/creatinine ratio).
Frequency of monitoring depends on acuity versus chronicity and the rate of progression, with nephrotic syndrome being more indolent than nephritic syndrome.

The value of serologic monitoring depends on the condition, for example, monitoring anti-GBM antibody titer assesses effectiveness of therapy in anti-GBM antibody disease, but C3 and antibody testing do not reflect disease activity in lupus nephritis.

feature.caption: Glomerulonephritis (GN): Natural History and Prognosis.
feature.feature_body:
Entity Natural History Prognosis
Minimal changea Progression to ESRD uncommon; complications of proteinuria 80% remission with steroids
Membranous GNb 1/3 remit, 1/3 progress, 1/3 indolent; male, age >55, proteinuria ≥10 g are risk factors No universally accepted protocol
Focal segmental glomerulosclerosisc Highly variable; etiology and pathologic variant ("tip" lesion, collapsing glomerular tuft) are risk factors ESRD ∼50% at 15 years, steroid response→better outcome
IgA nephropathyd Highly variable, may be indolent for years before converting to RPGN; azotemia/hematuria/proteinuria/biopsy are variables in risk ESRD 20%-40% over 5-25 years
Membranoproliferativee Hematuria/proteinuria, occasional NS, may convert to crescentic/RPGN ESRD 90% by 20 years
Postinfectious GNf Resolution usually a few months in children In adults, >50% with CKD by 5 years
Crescentic GNg ESRD/death in weeks-months without therapy; creatinine at time of diagnosis predicts renal survival, age >60 risk factor Renal survival <50% at 6 mo
Antiglomerular basement membraneh ESRD/death in months without therapy; pulmonary hemorrhage/respiratory failure; creatinine at time of diagnosis predicts renal survival 1-year survival 70%-90% but 60% ESRD
Antinuclear cytoplasmic antibodyi ESRD/death in months without therapy; respiratory tract hemorrhage ∼30% renal survival with aggressive therapy
SLE-proliferativej Can convert to RPGN, heightened risk of lupus flairs, variables include race, age, creatinine, pathology May have improved outcomes with oral mycophenolate or azathioprine
SLE-membranousk Might be similar to idiopathic membranous; risk of lupus flairs, thrombotic complications Indolent renal course, prognosis related to GFR at time of diagnosis
